Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National UG accommodation crisis has persisted for decades; needs practical solutions – Sulemana Braimah Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 21 November 2026 8:55am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Executive Director of the Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), Sulemana Braimah, says Ghana has failed to adequately address the longstanding accommodation crisis facing university students, warning that continued discussions without concrete action will not resolve the problem.
He has called for practical and sustainable interventions to address the shortage of affordable student accommodation, particularly at the University of Ghana, where concerns over hostel charges have intensified.
Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Braimah said the accommodation difficulties were not new, recalling that students were already struggling to secure places to stay when he enrolled at the University of Ghana in 2002.
His comments come amid growing concerns over proposed increases in hostel charges by the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL).
The initial proposal involved a 26 per cent increase in accommodation fees, but this was subsequently reduced following consultations with student leaders.
Addressing the role of the Rent Commissioner in the ongoing concerns, Mr Braimah acknowledged the official's interventions in accommodation-related matters, including issues involving ordinary tenants outside the university environment.
He said public officials who took their responsibilities seriously deserved recognition, even when the results of their work were not immediately visible to the public.
However, he argued that the central issue should not be whether the Rent Commissioner was being appreciated for his efforts, but rather how the country intended to resolve the accommodation challenges confronting university students.
“I think the most important point really is not about whether we appreciate what he is doing or not. I think it’s about the problem that confronts us, which is accommodation for university students,” he said.
Mr Braimah drew on his personal experience at the University of Ghana to illustrate how long the crisis had persisted.
He explained that he enrolled at the university in 2002 after completing teacher training and spent three years lodging with other people before securing an inner room in one of the university's main halls in his final year.
According to him, the accommodation crisis was already evident during his time at the institution, prompting the university to introduce a policy known as 'in-out-out-in' towards the end of his stay.
He said the situation demonstrated that the problem had existed for decades and should have been addressed through deliberate national interventions long before the current concerns over hostel fees emerged.
Mr Braimah expressed worry that Ghana appeared not to be taking the necessary steps to overcome the crisis, despite the years of public discussions surrounding student accommodation.
He admitted that he was uncertain how the country could immediately resolve the problem, given how long it had persisted.
He further cautioned that conversations and public commentary alone would not produce the desired results without practical measures to improve the availability and affordability of accommodation for students.
“So, as a nation, I believe we ought to have confronted this issue way back, and we are now in a situation where I don't know how we can immediately solve the problem. And it doesn't appear that we are taking the right steps towards redeeming ourselves from the crisis that we are in, because the talk will not solve any problem,” he added.
